verses.note: By describing the lights as tools that serve the earth, the verse removes them from the list of things to be feared or worshiped. The first lesson against idolatry comes before any command against it.

Laban speaks the name of the LORD, yet later his household keeps teraphim, household idols, which Rachel steals and Laban calls ‘my gods’ (Genesis 31:19, 30). Abraham's relatives knew the name of Abraham's God without belonging to him alone, which is part of why Joshua 24:2 remembers that the fathers beyond the River served other gods.

In one breath Laban describes a God who speaks to him in the night and restrains him, and then complains that his own gods have been carried off. The verse sets the living God who acts beside gods who cannot even keep their place on a shelf, the contrast Isaiah draws between gods that must be carried and the God who carries his people (Isaiah 46:1-4).

Laban's gods cannot reveal their own location or defend their own dignity. A woman sits on them, and they are hidden beneath a claim of impurity. The scene mocks idols by showing them helpless, a theme the prophets develop when they describe idols that must be fastened down so they do not topple (Isaiah 41:7).

Jacob's own household has carried foreign gods since Rachel took her father's household gods (31:19). The family of promise needs to be purged of idols before it can meet God, a pattern that runs through Israel's story.

Joseph receives an Egyptian name and marries into the priesthood of the sun god, yet the story shows him still naming God as the source of his gifts (verses 16, 51, 52). Living fully in a foreign culture, even under its names, does not require worshiping its gods, a pattern Daniel will repeat in Babylon (Daniel 1:7-8).

Pharaoh treats human beings as units of production and treats the desire to worship as idleness. The Bible's critique of Egypt is not only that it worships other gods but that it makes the state and its output into something absolute, to which every life must be sacrificed.
